displayQuote: A lie told often enough becomes the truth

meta.title: Who really said "A lie told often enough becomes the truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lenin, and not Goebbels either — neither has a source. The oldest hard citation is a 1946 US congressional publication that pinned it on Goebbels without evidence. There is no Russian original and no German one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A lie told often enough becomes the truth'?
meta.ogDescription: No Lenin source, no Goebbels source. The earliest datable attribution is a 1946 US congressional document — the quote is a Cold War artefact, not a Soviet or Nazi one.

answer.label: Nobody — no source exists for Lenin or Goebbels
answer.sourceLine: It is not in Lenin’s collected works, and the alternative credit to Joseph Goebbels is no better sourced. The earliest hard citation anyone has produced is a 1946 United States congressional publication that attributed it to Goebbels without evidence. So the attribution is not Soviet and not Nazi — it is an American Cold War artefact.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None — absent from the collected works
No Russian and no German exists

source.excerpt: There is no Russian original. Genuine Lenin quotations can be located in the Polnoe sobranie sochinenii, his complete works in fifty-five volumes. This sentence has no Russian text behind it at all — and no German text behind the Goebbels version either.
trail: Fabricated Lenin quotations are a documented Cold War genre — the ‘rope,’ ‘socialised medicine’ and ‘overripe fruit’ lines are all catalogued as inventions. This one sits in the same family: it circulates only through quotation aggregators, never with a citation Lenin, misattributed ↗.

The Goebbels version is filed as misattributed too, with the earliest citation being Publications Relating to Various Aspects of Communism (1946), a US House committee document — and the editorial note that no reliable source has ever been found Goebbels, misattributed ↗.

The absence of an original-language text is itself the evidence. A real Lenin line has a locatable Russian source; a real Goebbels line has a German one. This sentence has neither, in either language — it exists only in English.
source.excerptNote: Not a quotation but a finding — we will not invent a source text to fill this space. The missing original is the whole point: this saying has never existed anywhere but in English.
source.rightsNote: Rights here are indeterminate, because no author has ever been established — and that is the safest way to treat it. Lenin died in 1924 and Goebbels in 1945, so people assume the line is free to reproduce, but neither man wrote it, so neither death date settles anything. If you quote Hitler’s genuine ‘big lie’ passage for contrast, note that the German is public domain but the standard Manheim English translation of 1943 remains in copyright. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Lenin
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary, first head of the Soviet state
author.bio: Vladimir Lenin attracts fabricated quotations more reliably than almost any modern figure, because a cynical line about manipulating the public sounds like something he would say and few readers can check fifty-five volumes of Russian to find out. Several of the most-repeated ‘Lenin quotes’ in English were manufactured during the Cold War and have never been traced to him. This is one of them.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Two dictators are offered as the author and neither has a source. What makes this case unusual is that the genuinely related material says something quite different from the saying it is used to support.

items.why: Absent from the Polnoe sobranie sochinenii. It appears only in English-language quotation aggregators, never with a volume or page Wikiquote ↗.
The oldest attribution is a 1946 US House committee publication, which gave no citation. No German text has ever been produced Wikiquote ↗.

The große Lüge passage in Mein Kampf is real Hitler, but it is an antisemitic accusation: he claims his enemies tell a lie so colossal nobody could believe anyone would dare. It is not advice to repeat a lie until it becomes true, and it is not Goebbels.
His actual propaganda principle was to confine yourself to a few points and repeat them relentlessly — a rule about message discipline, not a claim that repetition manufactures truth.

misattribution.truthLine: No source for Lenin and none for Goebbels. The oldest datable attribution is a 1946 US congressional document, which makes this a Cold War invention rather than a Soviet or Nazi one the citation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is quoted to warn against propaganda, which is why the irony is so hard to ignore: a saying about repetition manufacturing truth has itself become true by repetition. It has been repeated into a Lenin quotation without a single citation ever changing hands.

The underlying claim is real, though, and has a name. Psychologists call it the illusory truth effect — the finding, first tested in 1977, that people rate repeated statements as more likely to be true simply because they have heard them before. The observation did not need a dictator to make it.
detailsBody: No Russian text exists — and genuine Lenin quotations always have one.
No German text exists — and genuine Goebbels quotations always have one.
Earliest datable attribution: 1946, a US House committee publication, uncited.
An 1869 English ancestor is sometimes cited — we could not verify it against the book, so we list it as a lead, not a finding.
The real phenomenon, the illusory truth effect, was first demonstrated experimentally in 1977.
context.pull: A saying about repetition making things true has become true by repetition.
